## The idea

A transcription can feel wrong while refusing to reveal where it is wrong.
Validation turns that broad unease into a smaller set of places to hear again.
A bar-length assertion finds missing time. A range check catches improbable
registers. A leap report points to intervals large enough to deserve comparison
with the source. None proves that a pitch is correct, but each removes a family
of routine mistakes from the search.

My rhythmic errors most often begin with a missing tie, a rest counted twice,
or a dotted value entered as though it were plain. All three change the amount
of time in a bar, so one exact total catches them without having to guess their
cause. Range and leap rules are less absolute: music can exceed either on
purpose. Report those cases as evidence for a person to review, not as edits
the program is authorised to make.

Once the structural checks are quiet, loop the suspicious bar beside the same
few seconds of the source. A short comparison lets you attend to attack time,
pitch, and release in separate hearings. Replaying an entire minute leaves too
many plausible locations competing for attention.

## Run this

The score stores each bar in a separate array, and each event carries a pitch,
local start, and duration. The validator stops execution when the meter is
broken. Large melodic motion produces a message instead, because an octave may
be surprising without being erroneous.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 80
use_synth :piano

bars = [
  [
    {note: 60, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 62, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 64, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
  ],
  [
    {note: 67, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 79, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0}, # octave leap: review
    {note: 76, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
  ]
]

define :validate_bar do |events, expected_beats|
  total = events.map { |event| event[:duration] }.sum
  raise "bar totals #{total}, expected #{expected_beats}" unless total == expected_beats

  events.each_cons(2) do |left, right|
    leap = (right[:note] - left[:note]).abs
    puts "REVIEW leap of #{leap} semitones" if leap >= 12
  end
end

define :play_events do |events|
  events.each do |event|
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.8
    sleep event[:duration]
  end
end

bars.each do |bar|
  validate_bar bar, 4.0
  play_events bar
end
```

Both bars account for four beats. In bar 2, the sudden rise from G4 to G5 is
audibly exposed, and the log reports its twelve-semitone size. The program has
located an observation; it has not decided whether the octave belongs in the
music.

## Change one thing

1. Shorten the last duration in bar 1 from 2.0 to 1.5 and run the buffer. The
   assertion stops playback before the malformed measure can become part of a
   longer listening pass. Read the reported total, restore the missing half
   beat, and confirm that bar 2 becomes reachable again.
2. Change note 79 to 80. The leap is now thirteen semitones, and the line rises
   to A-flat5. Add a range warning for notes below 48 or above 84. Two messages
   may describe the same event from different angles; keep both if each points
   to a distinct source question.
3. Loop `play_events bars[1]` three times and compare it with the corresponding
   source interval. On the first hearing, check attacks; on the second, pitches;
   on the third, releases. The repeated bar stays fixed while your attention
   changes.

## Why it works

Assertions encode properties that the representation must satisfy. In 4/4, an
ordinary complete bar accounts for four beats, including rests and any portion
of a tied continuation that occupies time. A pickup has a genuinely different
expected length, so give that measure its own value. Weakening every assertion
to tolerate one exception would remove the information the test was meant to
preserve.

Absolute event starts enable further checks. Sort events by start, reject
negative durations, and identify gaps or overlaps not present in the source. A
sequential array may be quicker to type because each duration implies the next
start. An absolute timeline is easier to compare with a score or recording
because one bad duration does not move every coordinate. Convert between the
forms in a helper rather than maintaining two hand-edited versions that can
disagree.

Warnings have a different role from assertions. A leap wider than an octave is
common in arpeggiated music and may be characteristic of the line. A plausible
range depends on instrument, singer, octave convention, and transposition. The
software can show you where an assumption was exceeded; the source and musical
context decide whether that event should change.

The milestone for this part is a thirty-to-sixty-second melody with a source
reference, bar-level data, validation helpers, and a separate expressive
renderer. Ruby syntax checks can confirm that the program parses, and automated
tests can inspect totals and ranges. They cannot confirm that the attacks match
the recording or that the shaped performance sounds convincing. Those claims
remain manual Sonic Pi work.

## Take it further

Add a validation report to the transcription from Lesson 45. List every bar
total, the overall note range, all leaps of twelve semitones or more, and each
`REVIEW` marker. Choose one suspicious bar and make a temporary three-stage
loop: neutral rhythm, strict pitches, then expressive rendering. Resolve each
failure or preserve it with an explanation tied to the source. A useful report
may still contain warnings; its value lies in showing why each surviving case
is understood.
